title: Who moved your hand off the hot pan?

scenes.heading: Who moved your *hand*?
scenes.narration: Your hand jumps off a hot pan before you decide anything. So who moved it? It wasn't your brain, at least not at first.

scenes.title: The obvious answer
scenes.narration: The obvious answer: your skin sends the heat to your brain, the brain decides, and tells your arm to pull back. That works for reaching a cup. But deciding takes time, and every moment on the pan means more damage.

scenes.title: The shortcut
scenes.narration: Here's the shortcut: your spinal cord, the thick bundle of nerves down your back. The heat signal reaches it first, and a small relay neuron sends it straight to your arm muscle. Your hand pulls back without waiting for the brain.

scenes.title: A reflex
scenes.narration: The brain still hears about it, just a moment later. That loop is a reflex. The catch? It doesn't think: it can make you drop whatever you're holding.

scenes.title: Remember
scenes.narration: So your spinal cord moved your hand, and your brain found out later. Have you ever dropped something because of a reflex? The full video is on the channel.

notes: The hot-stove reflex: receptors in the skin → sensory fiber → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle, "without actively thinking about it" (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, ch. 14 intro; Wikipedia, "Withdrawal reflex"). It is polysynaptic: one or more relay neurons sit between the sensory and the motor neuron.

Why it is not "thinking": the loop hand → spinal cord → arm is far shorter than the path up to the brain and back, and it needs no decision. The brain is informed in parallel, which is why you still feel it.
"It can make you drop whatever you're holding": an inference from the reflex being automatic; no study cited, so the voice says "can".
Simplified drawing: one fiber of each kind, one relay neuron. Real nerves carry thousands of fibers.
Educational only, no first aid or treatment advice. If a pain or an injury worries you, see a professional.
